title: Old age as a messenger
hookLine: a first gray hair in the bathroom mirror, and a king who asked his barber to watch for it
tomorrow: an old monk is told he can ease up. what does he say?

lines: TELL ME WHEN YOU SEE IT.
A GRAY HAIR IN HIS PALM.
cards: A first gray hair turns up in the mirror, and the reflex is to pluck it, dye it, or laugh it off. A sutta tells of King Makhadeva, who did something stranger.
He asked his barber: when you see gray hairs on my head, tell me. Years later, the barber did. The king had the gray hair plucked and laid in his palm, and he looked at it.
What do you do with news like that? Here's his answer, and an old psalm's answer beside it.

teach.b: The king gives the barber a village as a reward for the news.

Then he calls his eldest son and says: the messengers of the gods have appeared; gray hairs are seen on my head. He hands over the kingdom and goes forth to practice, asking his son to keep the custom and pass it on.
Elsewhere the Buddha names these messengers: an old person, a sick person, a dead person, each one sent to wake us up. So the gray hair isn't bad news.
It's a messenger, and its message is: what matters, while there's time? Now a neighbor who heard a messenger too.
A psalm in the Hebrew Bible, prayed by Jews and Christians, asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Shared: both see the passing of days as a teacher.
Neither treats age as only loss; both turn it toward wisdom and the heart.
Different, and honestly so: the psalm is a prayer, asking God to teach the counting.
In the sutta, nobody is asked; the gray hair is the messenger, and the king answers by going forth himself. Two old texts, two ways of listening, one gray hair in the palm.
And the custom, the sutta says, was meant to be passed down, from father to son.

how: Buddhist teachers often point to the 'divine messengers' (old age, sickness and death) as reminders to practice; some Buddhists reflect daily that they too are subject to ageing.

games.q: what does “old age as a messenger” mean?
o: a ghost believed to visit people near the end
growing older read as a reminder of what matters
a person who brings news to an elderly king

games.q: the king and the gray hair — tap the pairs.
p: the king who asked about gray hair
given the kingdom and the custom
teach us to number our days

s: King Makhadeva hid his first gray hair
he asked his barber to watch for it, then rewarded him for the news.
the Buddha names an old person as one of the divine messengers
along with a sick person and a dead person.
the psalm and the sutta say exactly the same thing
both treat the days as a teacher; the psalm asks God, the sutta's king answers by going forth.

games.q: your dad turns fifty and jokes darkly about being 'over the hill.' what would Makhadeva's story offer?
o: the gray is a messenger: what matters most, with the time ahead?
ignore it; age is just a number and means nothing at all.
he should hurry and quit his job, as the king left his kingdom.
games.why: the king welcomed the gray hair as a messenger and turned to what mattered to him; the message, not the exact step, is the point.

practice: Look at the back of one hand, slowly, for the whole sit: the lines, the veins, a scar, the knuckles. Look at it the way the king looked at the hair in his palm, without judging, as something that has worked hard for you.
Let whatever it says about time be a message, received kindly.

wordCard.voice: Old age as a messenger: a gray hair, a slower step, read not as bad news but as a reminder of what matters.

orig.note: Pali: devaduta, a divine messenger: old age, sickness and death.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the messenger, welcomed, not chased out of the mirror. Seven of nine.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 83 (Makhadeva Sutta: the king asks his barber to report gray hairs; gives him a village; tells his eldest son the divine messengers have appeared; goes forth; asks that the custom be continued)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.36 (Devaduta Sutta: the divine messengers, an old person, a sick person, a dead person)

sources.q: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
